# yyot v1 scope and release criteria ## State This is the revised v1 scope. The repository currently contains Git/Entire scaffolding only; no yyot application, deployed reviewer experience, or acceptance evidence exists yet. This document specifies required behavior, not implemented capabilities. Optimize for general browser-task capability and strong per-user security. Hermes Agent is the selected agent harness. Reuse its built-in messaging gateway and suitable tool integrations. TypeScript remains the user's preference for yyot-owned service and integration code where appropriate; run Hermes in its upstream runtime rather than reimplementing it in TypeScript. Hosting, browser/file capability, persistent storage, and per-user security integration still require validation. Slack is the v1 user interface, using Hermes' built-in Slack adapter. The user reported that Sahan approved Slack identity replacing the assignment's Google-only chatbot sign-in requirement. Reviewers use the deployed app in the demo Slack workspace through its invitation/entry link. Inference is owner-funded; reviewers need neither a checkout nor an OpenAI account. ## Architecture: shared team context and private personal execution One Slack app connects collaborative team conversations and isolated personal Hermes runtimes. The diagram describes logical responsibilities; the gateway and broker can be modules in the same trusted yyot service. Hosting and storage providers are not selected by this diagram. ```mermaid flowchart TD Slack["One yyot Slack app
Shared channels/threads and private DMs"] <--> Gateway["Trusted Slack gateway
Verify sender and conversation audience"] Gateway <-->|Shared conversation| Team["Team Hermes context
Partitioned by authorized channel/project audience"] Gateway <-->|Private DM routing| Broker["yyot authorization broker
Private dispatch and controlled publication"] Team -->|Request private work| Broker Broker -->|Owner-approved content and audience| Team Broker <-->|Sahan-authorized execution| Sahan["Sahan's isolated Hermes runtime
Private profile and durable data"] Broker <-->|Nishank-authorized execution| Nishank["Nishank's isolated Hermes runtime
Private profile and durable data"] ``` Collaborative team context is required in v1. Maintain two visibility domains: shared team context contains authorized channel/thread conversations, team decisions, shared goals/progress, and deliberately shared documents/results; personal context contains DMs, private memory, credentials, browser state, private files/artifacts, and private execution observations. Shared context must respect its actual workspace/channel/project audience; membership in a workspace does not reveal private-channel context. Collaborators can continue a shared discussion and plan without automatically sharing personal account access. The private boundary includes each user's full personal Hermes runtime and persistent personal data: DM transcripts/session databases, memory, learned skills derived from private work, private logs, credentials, browser state, working files, and private artifacts. Provision a separate runtime environment and private data volume per owner, backed by owner-scoped durable storage. The team conversation runtime gets only authorized shared context and has no direct access to personal homes, credentials, or browser sessions. Personal runtimes may read team context their owners are authorized to see. Never automatically copy personal transcripts, memory, screenshots, tool results, files, or learned skills into shared team memory. Private results use 1:1 Slack DMs until the owner approves the specific content and audience for sharing. Never expose platform/database/storage administrator credentials to model-generated code. Use one Slack bot with authenticated audience/sender routing, team Hermes context for designated shared channels/projects, and fresh personal profiles for private interactions. Keep the message sender, shared task/context audience, and private execution owner as separate application fields. A team request that needs personal accounts or files dispatches through an owner-authorized broker into that owner's private runtime. Another collaborator may contribute to the shared plan but cannot silently take over that execution, reuse its account authority, or approve on its owner's behalf. The team runtime receives safe status and owner-approved results rather than raw private observations. Keep bot credentials in the trusted receiving gateway rather than copying the bot token into personal runtimes. Admission must reject unprovisioned requesters instead of exposing a shared personal default. Hermes supports shared room/thread sessions and profile selection, but those settings do not implement per-request user authority or whole-runtime sandbox dispatch. Reuse the Slack adapter and routing primitives where they meet the boundary, and implement yyot-owned provisioning, private execution dispatch, access checks, and publication where necessary. Audit shared ingress logs, caches, queues, memory providers, and delivery-recovery stores: private personal payloads must not be retained in an unscoped shared store, while intentionally shared payloads retain their audience access controls. The trusted ingress necessarily handles messages in transit; Slack and configured model providers also process their respective message content. Pin and validate the Hermes version used. See [shared session settings](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions), [shared-bot profile routing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes), [profile routing non-goals](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/multiplexing-gateway/#non-goals), and [whole-runtime Docker deployment](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/docker/). ### Context and storage ownership | Data | Owner or audience | Access rule | | --- | --- | --- | | Team conversations, decisions, task progress, and team memory | Authorized workspace/channel/project audience | Scope retrieval and persistence to that audience. A shared runtime must not mix conversations with different access boundaries. | | Personal DMs, memory, learned skills, execution observations, and logs | Individual user | Keep within the owner's personal runtime and durable private storage boundary; never load automatically into team context. | | Credentials, browser sessions, working files, and private artifacts | Individual user | Only the owner's authorized private execution may use them. Personal runtimes cannot access another owner's storage. | | Deliberately shared documents and approved result copies | Explicit destination audience | Share only the approved content. The source private file and account remain private; sharing a result grants no account authority. | | Routing, run, approval, and recovery records | Verified sender, execution owner, and conversation audience recorded separately | Trusted yyot code enforces these fields. Persist private payloads within their owner's boundary and shared payloads within their audience boundary. | Keep durable history, task recovery state, and retained artifacts independently of a running worker's scratch disk. A restart must restore the same owner/audience boundaries. The team runtime and each personal runtime receive only scoped storage access; platform administrator credentials remain in trusted infrastructure. The concrete storage provider and artifact layout remain open. ### Shared task to private work to shared result 1. **Collaborate in the team thread.** Sahan requests a report and Nishank adds requirements. Both contributions enter the authorized shared task context. 2. **Authorize the private part.** If the report needs Sahan's account or private files, the broker verifies his authorization for that work, requests it privately if needed, and binds the work to his runtime. It supplies only team context he is allowed to read. 3. **Execute under Sahan's authority.** His personal Hermes runtime performs the work. Nishank can contribute to the team plan, but cannot redirect, resume, or approve Sahan's private execution through a thread follow-up. A changed private operation requires authorization covering that change; consequential actions receive their own owner confirmation. 4. **Return private output to Sahan.** Results and raw observations remain in his private boundary. Deliver the private result or a protected artifact link through his DM; raw observations are not automatically sent to Slack. The team receives only status appropriate for its audience, without private account details. 5. **Publish the selected result.** Sahan approves the specific content and destination audience. The broker publishes that content and records it in the corresponding team context. Changed content or audience requires fresh approval; source files, credentials, and raw observations remain private. This flow lets a team coordinate work that each account owner authorizes and performs through their own agent. Delegating account authority to another collaborator remains outside v1. Hermes integration points, browser/file execution, secure handoff, deployment, and restart persistence still need implementation and validation. ## Now: required behavior 1. **Execute general tasks and collaborate.** Understand natural-language requests across unfamiliar websites using one general execution engine. Discover, download, inspect, transform, and upload files when the task requires them. In shared team conversations, collaborators can contribute to a common task and reuse authorized shared decisions/progress across turns and restarts. Site-specific product scripts do not constitute general-task support. 2. **Collect and reuse access securely.** Collect passwords, API keys, TOTP setup keys, card details when required, and browser login/OAuth access through secure input or handoff outside chat and model inputs. Persist encrypted credentials and browser-session state, reuse supported access across tasks and fresh browser runs, generate TOTP codes outside model inputs, and let the owner revoke access. Revocation stops affected active execution and invalidates saved access/session state. 3. **Enforce ownership outside the model.** Derive the message sender and audience from verified Slack identity and authorized conversation membership. Bind every private run, browser/session, credential lookup, file operation, private artifact, personal memory/learned skill, and private-history retrieval to its owner's isolated runtime/data boundary. Bind team history, memory, and shared artifacts to their authorized audience. Another participant's follow-up can contribute shared task context but conveys no authority over a collaborator's private execution or accounts. Keep model-generated code isolated from platform master keys and other users' resources. 4. **Work in the background and recover.** Acknowledge requests promptly, give brief useful progress, clarify only material details, and provide private human login/verification handoff when necessary. Persist the goal and progress across access expiration or failures. Resume after the owner supplies what is needed, without blindly repeating completed consequential actions. Support cancellation and bounded execution. 5. **Confirm and verify.** Obtain the owner's confirmation before a concrete consequential action such as a purchase, external message, publication, or deletion. Changed action details require fresh confirmation. Verify the actual website state or intended artifact before declaring completion. Keep private account observations and results private until their owner approves specific content and its audience for sharing. Persist approved shared results with that audience scope; an approval to share a result does not grant account or filesystem access. These controls are application and execution-environment responsibilities. Hermes chat-session separation, profiles, allowlists, prompt instructions, separate browser profiles, or encrypted secret storage alone do not prove isolation or prevent observation leakage. Validate ownership across Hermes memory, session recall, learned skills, file/browser tools, and any enabled background jobs. Disable features whose data or authority cannot be scoped safely to their owner. Document and test the actual boundaries. ## Four deliverables | Deliverable | Completion criteria | | --- | --- | | Runnable repository | Dependency locks, setup instructions, environment-variable examples containing no secrets, and relevant verification instructions are included and exercised. | | Deployed reviewer experience | The backend and execution environment remain available without the developer's laptop. Two reviewers can enter through the Slack workspace invitation/entry link and use the app independently without local setup or an OpenAI account. | | Approximately two-minute yyoreel demo | A real request, secure access collection or handoff, and verified completion are shown. Include reuse/recovery where practical. Inspect the exported recording for exposed secrets before sharing it. | | Access-management and known-limits note | Explain verified identity/isolation, secret and browser-session storage, TOTP, reuse, revocation, observation leakage limits, and unsupported cases. Distinguish implemented and tested behavior from planned behavior. | ## Release evidence 1. Complete real tasks on at least two different websites through the same general engine, without preselected site-specific product flows; verify destination state rather than relying on the agent's completion message. 2. Find the intended requester-owned sandbox file and complete a browser upload. Also complete download, inspection/transformation, and upload as one task; verify the uploaded file is the intended artifact. 3. Collect access and a TOTP setup key through secure input, then demonstrate credential/TOTP reuse with a fresh browser run. Test session reuse separately, and verify revocation prevents subsequent reuse. 4. Exercise expired access or a controlled failure, provide the required owner input, and resume the persisted task successfully without replaying a completed consequential action. 5. Demonstrate two users contributing to the same shared task and reusing authorized team context after restart. Run adversarial checks: forged owner/account references, cross-user private file/artifact requests, another participant's thread follow-up, private-history/memory/learned-skill retrieval, and copied approval/handoff controls must not obtain another user's authority or private data. Verify concurrent private executions remain independent, a collaborator cannot approve an owner's action, and changed action details cannot reuse an earlier approval. Inspect transcripts, logs, memory-provider writes, and delivery/cache records for audience-scoped persistence. Demonstrate an owner-approved result becoming available to the team while its source private file, credentials, and raw observations remain protected; a shared turn must not automatically consume private state. Done means the required behavior is implemented, the four deliverables exist, and this evidence passes with honestly recorded limits. A video, a happy-path upload, or a deployed chatbot alone is not completion. If a required capability remains unsupported, report that gap explicitly rather than marking v1 complete. ## Later Additional interfaces beyond Slack, delegated use of another person's accounts, advanced cross-team memory/grants, and the configurable coding-agent-style approval-policy UX are deferred until after v1. Basic shared team conversation/task memory and explicit sharing of selected results are in v1. Hermes' built-in channel adapters can be evaluated when additional interfaces are needed. Ordinary owner confirmations remain in v1. ## Next Prove the execution path before broader implementation: one Slack app using Hermes' adapter, two users contributing to shared team context, owner-authorized dispatch into a full isolated personal Hermes runtime/data volume, file upload, durable team context and private history/artifacts across runtime restart, private login handoff, and explicit publication of an approved result back to the team. Validate conversation visibility, execution ownership, and publication separately rather than assuming shared sessions, profiles, or a terminal backend provide the boundaries. Then build the required behavior and collect the release evidence. Obtain the user's review before external submission or contacting the founders; this scope update authorizes neither.

# ADHD-Friendly Responses

Shape responses so the reader can act without retaining context.

## Response contract

1. For a task, make the first sentence an imperative, sub-two-minute action; put no reassurance or context before it. For a question, give the direct answer. Never announce this skill.
2. Number multi-step work: one action per step, five items per visible list. Shape plans as `Now` (up to five actions plus a done condition), `Later` (one line of phase names), `State`, and `Next`. Expand nothing else.
3. Restate the current step and progress. Surface wins, defer tangents, and use concrete time estimates.
4. For errors, state failure, evidence or cause, and fix. After three failed attempts, name the suspect assumption and ask one diagnostic question.
5. End unfinished work with one imperative, sub-two-minute action and nothing after it. If complete, end with the verified outcome.

## Exceptions

- Explain fully when asked, using skimmable headings.
- Confirm destructive or irreversible actions.
- Ask one question for material ambiguity.
- Let safety, accuracy, and explicit instructions override brevity.

## Pre-send check

Remove announcements, closing pleasantries, tangents, empty hedging, and buried wins. Ensure the first and last lines carry the action or outcome.

“Agent generates codes” means yyot’s software performs the authenticator app’s job during login.

- **Setup key:** the long-lived secret a website provides when enabling authenticator-based 2FA, commonly encoded in a QR code.
- **TOTP code:** the temporary numeric login code calculated from that secret and the current time.
- **Agent behavior:** when the website requests the authenticator code, an authorized tool calculates and submits the current code. The LLM need not know the secret or calculate the code itself.

The scope requires secure collection outside chat/model inputs, encrypted storage, code generation outside model inputs, reuse with a fresh browser run, and owner revocation. Its acceptance test explicitly includes collecting and reusing a TOTP setup key.

A beginner-friendly example: “You normally open your authenticator app and copy its current code. Here, yyot’s secure login tool does that step automatically.”

Your concern is valid: storing the TOTP setup secret lets the agent generate future codes without asking you. If an attacker controls the agent and its credential tools, they may gain that ability too.

Manually providing a current code keeps the setup secret with you and requires your involvement at login. But **it does not approve every later action**: the agent can keep using the authenticated session until it expires or is revoked. Sensitive actions still need separate confirmation.

L184: # OTPAuth
L185: 
L186: One Time Password library for Node.js, Deno, Bun and browsers.
L187: 
L188: It supports the generation and validation of HMAC-Based One-Time Passwords (HOTP) as specified in cite94†RFC 4226†datatracker.ietf.org and Time-Based One-Time Passwords (TOTP) as specified in cite95†RFC 6238†datatracker.ietf.org . Frequently used in Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) / Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) systems.
L189: 
L190: Tip
L191: You can try the library with the demo application available at cite96†otpauth.molinero.dev†otpauth.molinero.dev .

L196: ## Usage
L197: 
L198: This section presents an overview of the most common usage patterns, along with some security recommendations.
L199: ### cite97†Node.js / Bun†www.npmjs.com L200: 
L201:     import * as OTPAuth from "otpauth";
L202:     // import * as OTPAuth from "otpauth/slim"; // Slim build without bundled dependencies.
L203:     // import * as OTPAuth from "otpauth/bare"; // Bare build with no bundled crypto (requires providing a custom HMAC function).
L204: 
L205:     // Create a new TOTP object.
L206:     let totp = new OTPAuth.TOTP({
L207:       // Provider or service the account is associated with.
L208:       issuer: "ACME",
L209:       // Account identifier.
L210:       label: "Alice",
L211:       // Algorithm used for the HMAC function, possible values are:
L212:       //   "SHA1", "SHA224", "SHA256", "SHA384", "SHA512",
L213:       //   "SHA3-224", "SHA3-256", "SHA3-384" and "SHA3-512".
L214:       algorithm: "SHA1",
L215:       // Length of the generated tokens.
L216:       digits: 6,
L217:       // Interval of time for which a token is valid, in seconds.
L218:       period: 30,
L219:       // Arbitrary key encoded in base32 or `OTPAuth.Secret` instance
L220:       // (if omitted, a cryptographically secure random secret is generated).
L221:       secret: "REDACTED",
L222:       //   or: `OTPAuth.Secret.fromBase32("REDACTED")`
L223:       //   or: `new OTPAuth.Secret()`
L224:       // Custom HMAC function (required for bare build, optional otherwise).
L225:       // hmac: (algorithm, key, message) => Uint8Array,
L226:     });
L227: 
L228:     // Unless you know what you are doing, it is recommended to use the default
L229:     // values for the algorithm, digits, and period options, as these are the most
L230:     // common values used by most services.
L231: 
L232:     // Generate a cryptographically secure random secret.
L233:     // It is NOT recommended to use less than 128 bits (16 bytes).
L234:     let secret = new OTPAuth.Secret({ size: 20 });
L235: 
L236:     // Generate a token (returns the current token as a string).
L237:     let token = totp.generate();
L238: 
L239:     // Validate a token (returns the token delta or null if it is not found in the
L240:     // search window, in which case it should be considered invalid).
L241:     //
L242:     // A search window is useful to account for clock drift between the client and
L243:     // server; however, it should be kept as small as possible to prevent brute
L244:     // force attacks. In most cases, a value of 1 is sufficient. Furthermore, it is
L245:     // essential to implement a throttling mechanism on the server.
L246:     //
L247:     // For further details on the security considerations, it is advised to refer
L248:     // to Section 7 of RFC 4226 and Section 5 of RFC 6238:
L249:     //   https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4226#section-7
L250:     //   https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6238#section-5
L251:     let delta = totp.validate({ token, window: 1 });
L252: 
L253:     // Get the counter value (number of intervals since the Unix epoch).
L254:     // Useful for implementing techniques against token reuse during the validity
L255:     // period.
L256:     let counter = totp.counter();
L257: 
L258:     // Get the remaining milliseconds until the current token changes.
L259:     let remaining = totp.remaining();
L260:     // Convert to Google Authenticator key URI format.
L261:     // Usually the URI is encoded in a QR code that can be scanned by the user.
L262:     // This functionality is outside the scope of the project, but there are many
L263:     // libraries that can be used for this purpose, such as npmjs.com/package/qr
L264:     let uri = totp.toString();
L265:     //   or:      `OTPAuth.URI.stringify(totp)`
L266:     //   returns: `otpauth://totp/ACME:Alice?issuer=ACME&secret=REDACTED&algorithm=SHA1&digits=6&period=30`
L267: 
L268:     // Convert from Google Authenticator key URI format.
L269:     totp = OTPAuth.URI.parse(uri);
